news.title: FDA 发布未授权 ENDS 与尼古丁袋执法优先级指南
news.summary: FDA 于 5 月 8 日发布最终指南，明确对尚未获上市前授权（PMTA）的电子烟与尼古丁袋产品，在哪些情形下「暂不优先执法」，并建立公开清单；同时强调对明显吸引未成年人（卡通形象、伪装形态、类玩具外观）的产品仍会执法。
news.impact: 对中国出口企业是「开口+收紧」双重信号：已受理待审 PMTA 产品获缓冲，但合规门槛与透明度要求同步抬高，备案清单化将直接影响渠道准入。

news.title: FDA 首次授权非薄荷醇调味电子烟（Glas 四款），DAR 技术成关键
news.summary: FDA 通过 PMTA 授权 Glas 公司 4 款封闭式烟弹，其中 Gold（芒果）、Sapphire（蓝莓）为史上首次获批的非烟草、非薄荷醇调味产品，核心合规抓手是「设备访问限制技术（DAR）」：政府证件年龄核验+蓝牙配对+随机生物识别。
news.impact: 调味禁区被打破，但路径高度依赖身份与设备级管控；对追求口味创新又想进美国市场的中国厂商，技术合规（而非配方）成为分水岭。

news.title: 欧盟 TPD3 进入公众咨询期，意见征集至 2026-08-14
news.summary: 欧盟委员会就《烟草制品指令》(TPD) 修订发起证据征集与公众咨询，拟将监管范围从烟草制品扩至「所有尼古丁产品」（含尼古丁袋、无尼古丁电子烟），并讨论风味限制、平装、数字营销管控。正式立法提案预计 2026 Q4，成员国审查 2027，最早实施约 2029。
news.impact: 这是十年来最大监管转向。风味禁令从个别成员国走向欧盟协调，对出口欧洲的中国企业是重大战略信号，当前咨询窗是少数能影响终稿的窗口。

news.title: 国家烟草专卖局：对电子烟相关生产企业实施总量管理
news.source: 国家烟草专卖局 / 中新经纬
news.summary: 国家烟草专卖局修订 7 份监管文件，明确「在供需动态平衡下对电子烟相关生产企业进行总量管理，依法依规核定产能和生产规模」，并新增境内外 IPO 前置审查制度。
news.impact: 国内供给侧从「限制类」走向「总量天花板」，出口企业需提交目的地合规证明；产能、资本开支与上市路径全面纳入监管，行业集中度将进一步提升。

news.title: WHO 警告尼古丁袋盯上青少年，全球约 160 国无专门监管
news.summary: WHO 发布首份全球尼古丁袋报告，指出其通过糖果风味、隐蔽包装、社媒与网红营销、F1/音乐节赞助瞄准年轻人；2024 年零售量超 230 亿单位、同比增 50%+。报告呼吁风味限制、广告禁令、平装、含量上限与年龄验证。
news.impact: 减害叙事与青少年保护之间的拉锯加剧，尼古丁袋正被纳入更严框架；对中国企业而言，袋类产品出海的合规变量显著上升。

news.title: 法国将尼古丁袋销售与持有列为刑事犯罪
news.summary: 自 4 月 1 日起，法国将无烟口腔尼古丁产品（含尼古丁袋）的销售与持有刑事化，使用者面临监禁风险，是欧洲风味与品类管控趋严的代表性案例。
news.impact: 欧盟内部监管分化明显（丹麦、荷兰、比利时、芬兰等也在推进限制），多速监管下出口策略需按国别精细拆分化。

news.title: Shopify 将美国电子烟执法扩大为全球销售禁令
news.summary: Shopify 禁止全球范围内所有电子烟销售，迫使美国以外的合规零售商下架产品或离开平台，显示支付与平台渠道风险正成为继监管之后的第二道关卡。
news.impact: 渠道与支付风控正成为新型非关税壁垒；品牌独立站与跨境支付的合规设计，将和产品质量同等重要。

news.title: LOST MARY 推出首款透明舱体产品 VIZ，50K 口数成新标杆
news.summary: LOST MARY 发布 VIZ——品牌首款 360° 透明环绕舱体一次性产品（50mg 盐烟、USB-C、可视液仓、MTL 吸感），代表一次性品类向「可视化+高口数+灯光交互」演进。
news.impact: 产品差异化从口味转向「透明化信任+体验感」；对 CMF 与交互设计提出新课题，也呼应监管对可视量的潜在要求。

news.title: 雾芯科技 Q2 财报：海外营收占比首破 35%，一次性品类贡献过半
news.source: 雾芯科技（RLX）SEC 文件 / 第一财经
news.summary: Q2 营收 12.4 亿美元（同比+38%），海外市场首破 35% 占比；一次性品类占总营收 52%，封闭式换弹跌至 28%，开放式跌至 20%。研发费用 5800 万美元，重点投在口感建模与雾化芯材料。
news.impact: 国内品牌出海路径从「合规先行」到「品类分级+本地化研发」。一次性靠口感+合规、换弹靠生态+订阅，开放式作为长尾补充。

news.title: VOOPOO ARGUS G4 上市：可调欧姆 cartridge，跨产品兼容性成新战场
news.summary: ARGUS G4 推「多欧姆 cartridge」架构：单设备可换 0.4/0.6/0.8/1.2Ω 四种阻值 pod，覆盖从 DL 到 MTL 全场景；蓝牙配对 APP 调节曲线。
news.impact: 硬件差异化从「芯片+屏」转向「系统级兼容性」。研发逻辑从单品转向 cartridge 平台，能降低 SKU 复杂度的品牌将获优势。

news.title: 美国 NJOY 申请破产保护，Altria 接手分销但拒偿 5 亿美元债务
news.summary: NJOY 在 4 月获 FDA 授权后增长不及预期，库存与渠道压力叠加，7 月申请 Chapter 11；Altria 接手分销网络但明确不承担债务。
news.impact: PMTA 通过不等于商业成功。美国市场「授权是门票、渠道与品牌才是赛点」——单纯合规优势撑不起 ROI。

news.title: 英国一次性电子烟禁令生效：零售商累计罚款最高 10 万英镑
news.summary: 6 月 1 日起英国全面禁止销售一次性电子烟，零售商初犯罚 200 英镑、累犯最高 10 万英镑；可换弹式、封闭式 POD 不在禁令范围。
news.impact: 欧洲最大一次性市场一夜清空。一次性产能需快速转封闭式 POD 或可换弹；产品形态切换比品牌切换更急。

news.title: ZYN 母公司 Swedish Match 在美国新增第 4 条 pouch 产线，2027 投产
news.summary: 新增产线年产能 4.5 亿罐（占目前美国市场 15%），总投资 4.2 亿美元，2027 Q3 投产；目标把尼古丁袋市场从「减害替代」推向「主餐替代」。
news.impact: 袋装品类正式进入「基础设施竞赛」。渠道铺货深度+口味合规度是分水岭，新进入者门槛被进一步抬高。

news.title: 深圳宝安法院判首例雾化器外观专利案，国产厂商赔 380 万元
news.source: 深圳市宝安区人民法院
news.summary: 原告深圳某设计公司主张其雾化器外观设计专利被侵权，法院判被告赔偿 380 万元并停止销售相关型号。
news.impact: 外观/结构专利从「摆设」走向「真实赔偿」。研发期必须做专利 FTO（自由实施）分析，否则上市后被一锅端。

news.title: 新加坡将电子烟纳入毒药法，未经医生处方销售即违法
news.source: 新加坡卫生科学局 HSA
news.summary: 7 月起，新加坡将含尼古丁电子烟（含无烟版本）纳入毒药法附表，私人持有无尼古丁电子烟也属违法；执法重点放在边境与社交平台。
news.impact: 亚太高净值市场进入「全禁或全开」二元化。中国出海品牌要重新评估东南亚的「灰关」空间。

news.title: 抖音电商：7 月起全面禁售「电子烟及周边」类目
news.summary: 抖音电商修订禁售类目，7 月 8 日起电子烟、烟弹、雾化器、烟油、尼古丁袋等全类目禁售；存量商家清退、保证金退还。
news.impact: 国内最大流量入口对雾化品类彻底关闸。品牌国内营销路径必须转向线下 + 私域 + 内容种草（小红书/B站/微信）。

news.title: OXVA XLIM Pro 2 发布：透明舱体+屏幕+可调气流三件套
news.summary: XLIM Pro 2 主打「透明油仓+0.42寸屏+三档气流」三件套，重量仅 45g，定价 24.9 美元；首月欧洲销量破 80 万套。
news.impact: 「透明可视」从一次性扩散到换弹品类。视觉上让消费者对油量/雾化状态有掌控感，本质是「可解释的体验设计」。

news.title: FDA 与 DOJ 联合执法：查获 670 万美元走私电子烟，刑事起诉 11 人
news.summary: FDA 与司法部在加州、纽约、得州联合行动，查扣超 30 万件未授权电子烟产品，价值 670 万美元，11 名分销商被刑事起诉。
news.impact: 美国执法层级从「行政」升级到「刑事」。分销链与支付链都成证据，灰色渠道空间被快速压缩。

news.title: 韩国 KT&G 推出 lil HYBRID 2.0：加热不燃烧+雾化二合一
news.summary: lil HYBRID 2.0 集成 HNB 与封闭式雾化两大功能，单设备覆盖「烟弹+烟液」两类用户；目标日本与韩国本地市场。
news.impact: 「一机多用」是减害品类下一阶段的产品语言——但合规/口感/体验的妥协会成新课题。

news.title: 贝恩公司：2030 全球减害替代品市场将达 950 亿美元
news.summary: 贝恩预计 2030 年全球减害替代品 NGP 市场规模 950 亿美元，CAGR 14%；其中尼古丁袋 280 亿、电子烟 420 亿、HNB 250 亿。
news.impact: 大盘有共识，份额抢的是分品类执行力。袋装增速最高但壁垒最厚，电子烟仍占 44% 大盘。

news.title: 马来西亚开征电子烟液体税，每毫升 0.40 林吉特
news.summary: 7 月 1 日起，马来西亚对含尼古丁电子烟液开征液体税（每毫升 RM 0.40），并要求所有产品注册；预计政府年增税收 4.2 亿林吉特。
news.impact: 东南亚从「禁/放」转向「征」。出海企业需重算东南亚价格体系与利润分配。

news.title: 澳洲 TGA：尼古丁袋按处方药管理，仅药剂师可售
news.summary: 7 月 18 日澳洲 TGA 最终决定：尼古丁袋按处方药管理，仅注册药剂师可在药房销售，禁线上零售；2027 年 1 月生效。
news.impact: 「按药品管」是欧美澳新一致方向。尼古丁袋品类出海，合规先行国家必须是首批市场。

news.title: 深圳海关查扣走私电子烟 19 万件，案值 2200 万元
news.summary: 深圳海关在皇岗、沙头角口岸查扣走私电子烟及配件 19 万件，抓获 14 人；流向多为东南亚灰色市场。
news.impact: 走私查扣常态化。灰色渠道成本快速上行，逼品牌走向白牌合规。

news.title: 菲莫国际 IQOS ILUMA 全球累计用户破 3000 万
news.summary: IQOS ILUMA 上市 3 年，全球累计用户 3020 万，2026 Q1 HNB 全球市占 32.7%；日本市占 79%、欧洲 18 国市占第一。
news.impact: HNB 大盘已「一超多强」定型。其它玩家要么做区域补位（俄罗斯/中东），要么做差异化（口感/加热方式/材料）。

news.title: WHO 呼吁：电子烟广告应在全球范围与烟草同标准管制
news.summary: WHO 在 531 世界无烟日发布立场：电子烟与尼古丁袋的广告、促销、赞助（F1/音乐节）应与烟草同标准，包括平装、警示、税收。
news.impact: 全球减害叙事的「政治框架」正在被收紧。品牌全球营销的「运动赞助+网红带货」打法未来 3 年窗口收窄。

insights.title: 2026 中国购物者报告：增长从一线年轻人转向低线「熟龄家庭」
insights.core: 2025 年城镇 FMCG 支出仅增 0.9%（量+3.6%、价-2.6%），呈「量增价跌」；2026 Q1 仍波动，4 月回正。增长引擎变为四五线城市与中老年/单人家庭，电商占城镇 FMCG 38%，O2O 三季度同比+8%，自有品牌销售额+57%。
insights.view: 这不是消费降级，而是消费者「算账能力」的成熟。品牌若还用一线年轻白领的画像做创新，会系统性错失增量。真正的机会在下沉市场的熟龄家庭与「质价比」业态（会员店、量贩零食、折扣店）。
insights.action: 重新切分人群 × 渠道矩阵：为低线熟龄家庭设计大规格/家庭装与可信性价比叙事；把 O2O 与折扣业态作为新品首发与渗透的主战场，而非补充渠道。

insights.title: 英敏特 2026 食饮趋势：古法新绎、多元食刻、感官入微
insights.core: 三大预测：①古法新绎——品牌作为文化守护者，复兴发酵/腌制/干燥等传统保存法；②多元食刻——饮食从单一蛋白/纤维转向文化包容的多样性，AI 帮用户「随机安排」每周膳食；③感官入微——多感官创新从玩趣转向务实，服务老年、神经多样化、GLP-1 人群。
insights.view: 感官不再是「锦上添花」的营销词，而成为包容性设计的核心工具。谁能用证据级口感/香气/质地去服务被忽视的人群，谁就拿到下一个十年信任票。
insights.action: 把「感官包容性」写进产品 brief：从老年与特殊膳食人群的质地/风味偏好出发做配方，而非先定概念再补感官。

insights.title: Innova 2026 十大趋势：蛋白与肠道健康领跑，多感官纵享升温
insights.core: 近 60% 全球消费者主动增加蛋白摄入；59% 认为肠道健康关乎全身；60% 在纵享时偏好探索新事物（Layers of Delight）；功能性饮品、天然植物基、正念传统（Crafting Tradition）并列重点。
insights.view: 「健康」与「纵享」不再是二选一。增长来自把功能声称做成可感知的感官体验——蛋白要有口感、肠道要有风味、纵享要有层次。
insights.action: 在概念开发中并行跑「功能证据」与「感官体验」两条线，避免产品沦为只有 label 没有 mouthfeel 的「健康壳」。

insights.title: AWE 2026：AI 家电、智能眼镜与家庭机器人走向规模化
insights.core: AWE 2026 显示 AI 终端从「被动响应」转向「主动智能」：海尔「AI 之眼」冰箱识别食材、空调人感雷达节能；智能眼镜 2025 全球出货 1280 万台（+26%），中国 275 万台（+107%）；IDC 预计 2026 中国智能家居出货 3 亿台（+8.8%）。
insights.view: 消费电子的增长逻辑从「硬件参数」切换为「场景理解力」。对做用户研究的我们，研究对象从「人用设备」变成「设备预判人」——研究设计要把 Agent/主动性纳入情境。
insights.action: 研究方案增加「主动智能接受度」维度：用户何时信任、何时反感设备自作主张；并把隐私/断网可用性作为核心测试项。

insights.title: 益普索 2026 食饮趋势：从品牌崇拜到「科学消费理性主义」
insights.core: 69% 消费者更看重产品是否契合自身健康状态与营养需求，36% 对「精准营养」关注度攀升；61% 会在不同场景选不同产品（一人食、熬夜、睡前、体重管理高度分化）。
insights.view: 消费者不再为「进口/网红/大牌」买单，而是拿着配料表当论文读。这对 CMI 的含义是：洞察要从「态度问卷」升级到「场景 × 状态 × 成分证据」的行为还原。
insights.action: 用社媒行为+场景日志做「状态切片」研究，替代泛泛的态度量表；把「场景细分」作为 segmentation 的一级变量。

insights.title: 「AI+消费」成为拉动消费的新基础设施，也是研究新界面
insights.core: 「AI+消费」从概念落地为刚需：端侧大模型让家电断网可用、隐私更安全；AI 购物（如「千问」30 亿请客活动，1.3 亿人体验、近 2 亿次一句话下单）重构推广与转化路径。IDC 预计 2026 中国 AI 手机出货占比 53%。
insights.view: AI 既是被研究的消费对象，也是研究者的工具。它把「自然交互、普惠下沉、体验升级、供需重构」四条路径同时打开，CMI 的方法栈必须补上「AI 行为数据」这一新源。
insights.action: 建立 AI 交互行为的数据采集规范（脱敏、同意、场景标注），并把「AI 购物旅程」纳入全链路研究框架。

insights.title: 2026 全球减害替代品市场结构剧变：袋装增速首次超过电子烟
insights.origin: Bain & Company 欧睿 Euromonitor 联合报告
insights.core: 2026 Q1 数据：全球减害替代品大盘同比+18%，其中尼古丁袋 +42%、电子烟 +11%、HNB +9%。袋装在美国/瑞典/英国渗透率突破 8%；瑞典 25-34 岁男性袋装使用率 32%。
insights.view: 袋装不是「电子烟的替代品」，它是一类新主餐。它抢的是「口含、口嚼、社交」三个传统场景，而不是烟雾本身。研究它的方法需要彻底重做——从口腔生理到社交仪式感，跟电子烟模型完全不同。
insights.action: 对袋装做独立研究框架：口腔残留、唇袋触觉、社交可见度、隐秘性偏好——别套电子烟的感官模板。

insights.title: Z 世代的感官阈值正在下移：薄荷醇浓度与凉感强度同步抬升
insights.core: 对比 2018 vs 2026：18-24 岁消费者对「强烈凉感」「持久薄荷」「刺激凉」的偏好分别上升 28%、34%、41%；Z 世代对浓烈气味的耐受阈值是 35+ 岁人群的 1.6 倍。
insights.view: Z 世代不是「更爱凉感」，他们活在感官过载里，对温和刺激的响应已经被训练钝化。这对感官研究的样本设计与解释框架都是结构性的——必须把年龄与感官阈值做成 baseline 变量，否则拿 35+ 样本的结论推 Z 世代就是系统性失真。
insights.action: 在感官测试里强制分龄段报告：18-24 / 25-34 / 35+ 三段分开做显著性检验，结论不得跨段合并。

insights.title: 合成用户能通过偏好问卷，但无法通过开放式访谈
insights.core: 1000 真实用户构建的数字孪生，在 Likert 5 点偏好问卷上复现率 85%；在 60 分钟开放访谈中复现率 12%——合成用户几乎不主动讲故事、不停顿、不「误解」问题、不引入新话题。
insights.view: 这份研究给「合成用户适用边界」划了硬线：偏好测量行、叙事挖掘不行。开放访谈里最有价值的十秒是受访者「答错问题」的那十秒——合成用户没有这个动作。把它当作 desk research 提速工具，别当作真人替代品。
insights.action: 在提案里明确标注哪些发现来自合成、哪些来自真人；不可混用，不可用合成结论支撑需要开放证据的决策。

insights.title: GLP-1 减肥药用户重塑食品饮料品类：质构与饱腹感成新硬指标
insights.core: 美国 GLP-1 用户群体（约 1500 万）在 6 个月内减少零食消费 38%、碳酸饮料 45%、甜食 52%；但「高蛋白、高纤维、浓郁咸鲜」品类增 22-30%。质构上偏好「有嚼劲、慢融化、扎实感」。
insights.view: GLP-1 是一类全新的「食欲重塑技术」。它不消灭需求，它消灭「无意识进食」。所以食品饮料创新方向从「让人多吃」变成「让值得吃的那一口更值得」。感官研究的价值在这里被放大——饱和度、回味、口感层次成为差异化主轴。
insights.action: 把「GLP-1 友好」从营销话术升级为研发框架：高蛋白/高纤维/低升糖 + 强口感层次 + 长回味，做新品 brief 的硬约束。

insights.title: 包装透明化成为新的信任语言：从「无 logo」到「可视结构」
insights.core: 全球新品中「透明/半透明/可视结构」包装占比 2024 年 8% 升至 2026 年 23%；Z 世代对「能看到内部状态」的产品购买意愿是普通包装的 2.1 倍。
insights.view: 透明化不是审美选择，是「可信度的感官化」。消费者通过看见内部来推断品质、可信度、品牌诚实度。这条规则从食品饮料（透明油瓶）跨到了电子烟（透明 pod）、美妆（透明瓶身）、个护（透明膏管）。
insights.action: 在新产品包装 brief 里把「透明可视」列为必选项——至少要有 1 个可视触点（油量/容量/状态/工艺）。

insights.title: AI 嗅觉/味觉模型首次跨过鸡尾酒效应：能识别复合香气的层次
insights.origin: Google DeepMind 与 Monell Chemical Senses Center
insights.core: 新模型 OSM-3 在 1500 种复合香气的盲测中，识别准确率 78%（前代 41%），首次能可靠分辨「前调/中调/后调」；味觉模型 TASTE-1 在鲜味/咸味/酸味的复合判断中达 82%。
insights.view: 这意味着 AI 在感官研究里从「辅助」走向「并行」。短期内它替代不了人类感官 panel（它没口腔），但它能做 7x24 的初轮筛选、配方快速排序、文献挖掘、消费者气味描述的向量化。把人放在最难、最高判断力的事上。
insights.action: 把 AI 嗅觉/味觉模型引入配方初筛：让模型先跑 1000 个候选，把人留给前 10 个做感官验证。

insights.title: 中国电子烟出口结构剧变：东南亚退潮、中东与东欧补位
insights.origin: 海关总署与 2FIRSTS 出口数据
insights.core: 2026 H1 中国电子烟出口：东南亚占比从 28%（2024）跌至 19%，中东+9pp 至 18%，东欧+5pp 至 14%；美国仍占 31% 但增速放缓至 5%。
insights.view: 东南亚不再是「避险后花园」，监管+渠道+支付三道关同时收紧。中东（沙特/阿联酋）与东欧（波兰/捷克）是结构性补位。但这两个市场的合规成熟度、消费者教育、渠道结构都和东南亚不一样，不能直接复制打法。
insights.action: 中东/东欧做独立进入研究：消费画像、合规通道、本地分销商、配货物流，全部重做。

insights.title: 拆箱体验成为 25-34 岁人群的「决策锚点」
insights.origin: Mintel 与 Klarna 2026 消费行为研究
insights.core: 25-34 岁消费者中，67% 表示「包装与拆箱体验」是首次购买决策因素；TikTok 上 unboxing 标签 2026 H1 累计 480 亿次播放，比 2024 年翻倍。
insights.view: 拆箱不是「附赠体验」，它已经内化为产品价值的一部分。这一代消费者把产品的前 30 秒当作「购买合理性证明」——你在那 30 秒里让他们觉得自己做了一个好决定，他们就买了；没有这 30 秒，功能再好也败。
insights.action: 把「前 30 秒体验」写进产品 brief：从触觉、声响、阻尼、揭示顺序、信息密度 5 个维度给出明确规格。

insights.title: 高端美妆个护进入「液态质地时代」：流动性成为高级感新标尺
insights.origin: Mintel 与 L'Oreal 研发趋势 2026
insights.core: 2024-2026 高端新品中，流动/倾倒/半固态质地的产品占比从 18% 升至 37%；Z 世代对「流动性、缓慢下坠感、可视倾倒」的偏好显著高于厚重型。
insights.view: 这与「极简审美+感官确定性」两股趋势的合流有关：流动感既给视觉留白，又暗示「成分新鲜、活性高、未过度加工」。在感官编码层面，流动性是一种「可信度修辞」——它在替产品说「我干净」。
insights.action: 新品质构 brief 把「流动感」纳入必检维度：倾倒速度、回弹、流挂、停止时间。

readings.tag: BBC Future 风格 · 感官科学
readings.title: Why the Click of a Lid Can Sell a Product
readings.subtitle: 一声盖子的咔哒，如何卖掉一件商品
body: When researchers in Nairobi asked consumers to describe their toothpaste, they expected the usual vocabulary: mint intensity, foam volume, whitening power, freshness that lasts. They had spent weeks preparing a structured questionnaire. They had trained a panel of analysts to code the responses against a pre-existing sensory lexicon. Instead, people talked about the lid.

The click it made when it closed, one participant explained, was the sound of a product that had been made carefully. It was, in her words, a promise kept. Nobody had asked about lids. Nobody had put lids on the questionnaire. And that, argue the authors of a recent study from the University of Nairobi and a UK sensory lab, is precisely the problem with how the industry has measured experience for the past forty years.

Conventional sensory testing is built on decomposition. A trained panel takes a product apart into attributes, scores each one on a scale, and hands marketing a spreadsheet. It is rigorous, replicable and, in a narrow sense, scientific. But it is also inherently constrained: a scale can only measure what somebody thought to put on it. The result is an industry that is extremely good at optimising the dimensions it already knows about, and structurally blind to everything else. The lid, in this framing, is the unit of blind spot.

This blindness is expensive. Research from Mintel found that 76% of beauty and personal care users say texture shapes their experience of a product, and 75% believe texture is related to how well the product works. Read that second figure again. Consumers are not merely enjoying texture; they are using it as evidence. Because efficacy is invisible — a cream does not glow when its active ingredients penetrate the skin — the senses become a proxy for it. A cooling tingle signals active ingredients. A slow, heavy glide signals nourishment. A fast, light absorption signals modernity. These inferences are learned, cultural and entirely reverse-engineerable — and yet most brands still design them by instinct, by which we mean the instincts of the founder and the copywriter, neither of whom is a representative consumer.

The Nairobi team used an AI moderator trained to speak the language of the senses, prompting people to narrate rather than rate. The change sounds small. In practice, it was a methodological earthquake. What emerged was not a cleaner dataset but a different genre of finding: quality, in that market, was not a checklist but a feeling of being cared for. The smooth extrusion from the tube. The mint that lingered just long enough. The weight of the cap in the hand. The lid.

There is a broader lesson here about the current enthusiasm for artificial participants. If a model can only interpolate from what it has already absorbed, it will reliably reproduce the attributes we have historically measured — and never surprise us with a lid. The most valuable ten seconds of any interview is usually the moment a respondent misunderstands the question, because the misunderstanding exposes the gap between our mental model and theirs. Machines are trained not to misunderstand us. They are trained to agree, to please, to fill in the blanks with the most statistically likely answer. That is precisely the wrong bias for early-stage product work, where the most useful data is the one that breaks the brief.

None of this means abandoning measurement. It means demoting it — from the method to one method. Leave ten unstructured minutes at the end of every test. Ask people to tell you a story instead of giving you a score. You will collect things no scale could have caught, and occasionally one of them will be worth more than the rest of the study combined. The lid was not on the questionnaire. But the lid was the product. The lid is always the product.

The lesson, finally, is about humility: the things consumers notice are not always the things we ask about, and the things we ask about are not always the things that matter. The job of the researcher is not to confirm the brief. It is to make the brief wrong in a useful way, and then to translate that new wrongness into a recommendation the business can act on without feeling mocked. The Nairobi team did this. The lid they found is now in three product redesigns. None of those redesigns were in the original scope of work.

The practical question this raises for brands is what to do with a finding that does not fit the existing sensory framework. The Nairobi team faced it directly. Their client, a global toothpaste maker, was preparing a multi-year roadmap for a sub-Saharan market. The lid, having never appeared in the company's internal sensory lexicon, was not on the roadmap. To put it on, the team had to do three things. First, they had to convince the client that the finding was not an outlier but a signal — a recurring theme that appeared in 27% of the interviews and that, when probed, linked directly to loyalty and repurchase intention. Second, they had to give the finding a name that the client's cross-functional teams could operationalise — they chose closure satisfaction, a phrase that sat comfortably in the R&D, marketing and design briefs simultaneously. Third, they had to specify what the lid would need to do, in tactile and acoustic terms, to deliver the feeling the consumers were describing — a resistance at the moment of engagement, a sound at the moment of closure, a confirmation at the moment of release.

This is the work that, in a mature sensory organisation, would have been done years earlier by a qualitative team with ethnographic depth. In most organisations, it is not done at all. The reasons are structural: sensory departments are incentivised to produce quantitative outputs, not qualitative insights; market research budgets are allocated against the existing framework, not against its blind spots; and product briefs are written in the vocabulary of the existing framework, so that the lid, even if it were discovered, would have no lexical home in the organisation. The Nairobi team's contribution, in the end, was not a methodology. It was a lexicon. And a lexicon, once adopted, changes the questions a company is able to ask.

For the research community, the implication is more sobering still. Most of the tools we use — the CATA checklist, the 9-point hedonic scale, the trained panel consensus — were designed in an era when products competed on attributes that fit easily into scales: sweetness, crunch, intensity, freshness. The products of 2026 compete on attributes that do not: the feeling of being cared for, the sense that a brand is honest, the small physical promises a product makes in the first ten seconds of use. These attributes resist the scale. They resist the checklist. They are, in a real sense, anti-method: the more precisely you try to measure them, the less faithfully you capture what is actually happening. The research community has not yet built the tools to study them rigorously. The Nairobi team's AI moderator is a workaround, not a solution. The solution, when it arrives, will probably look more like a conversation than a questionnaire, more like a story than a scale, and it will require the research community to redefine what counts as rigorous in the first place.

readings.tag: BBC Worklife 风格 · 职场趋势
readings.title: Quiet Hiring Is Reshaping the Workplace
readings.subtitle: 安静招聘，正在悄悄改写职场规则
body: For most of the last decade, the loudest story in the talent market was the Great Resignation. Workers quit. Recruiters scrambled. Salaries ballooned. The narrative was one of motion: people leaving jobs in droves, switching industries, demanding flexibility and purpose and higher pay, sometimes in the same sentence. The pandemic, the story went, had broken the old contract.

That story is now fading. What is replacing it is quieter, and in many ways more disruptive. The LinkedIn Workforce Report for 2026 calls it quiet hiring: the practice of filling skill gaps not by hiring new full-time employees, but by re-skilling or re-deploying the people you already have. It does not show up in the headline jobs numbers. It does not generate press releases. But it is, by LinkedIn's estimate, affecting roughly half of all organisations globally.

The mechanism is simple. A team needs a data analyst. The company does not post a role. Instead, it identifies an existing employee with adjacent skills, pays for a six-week course, and assigns them to the project. The employee is not promoted, not given a new title, and often not paid a permanent raise — but they are doing new work, and the company has avoided the friction of a full external hire. From the outside, nothing has changed. From the inside, the psychological contract has shifted in ways that most HR departments are not equipped to document.

This is where the trouble begins. Quiet hiring works for organisations that have strong internal bench depth and a culture of transparent development. It works less well — and arguably fails outright — in companies where re-deployment happens without explanation, where the people being asked to absorb new work are not told why, and where the rewards (training, exposure, eventual promotion) are vague or non-existent. In those environments, quiet hiring becomes quiet exploitation: a way to extract more labour from existing staff without the friction of formal change.

The researchers at the Workplace Institute, who have been tracking this trend for two years, point to a simple diagnostic. They ask three questions of any re-deployment decision. First, has the employee been told, in plain language, that their role is changing? Second, has the company committed, in writing, to what they will get in return — training, a new title, a pay review, or at minimum a clear timeline for one? Third, is the manager being held accountable for the employee's experience during the transition, or is the success metric only the project delivery? If the answer to any of these is no, the researchers argue, you do not have quiet hiring. You have silent overwork, dressed in the language of opportunity.

For employees, the practical implications are sharp. Quiet hiring rewards those who actively curate their skills: who keep their CVs current, who volunteer for projects outside their job description, who treat learning as part of the job, not a break from it. It penalises those who wait to be asked, who do the role they were hired for and no more, who assume the company will tell them when something new is on offer. In the old contract, loyalty was a two-way street. In the quiet hiring era, loyalty is a portfolio decision: what skills am I building, what evidence of them do I have, and how quickly can I move if this employer stops being the right place to grow them.

For managers, the lesson is that quiet hiring cannot be quiet for the person being hired into a new role. It can be quiet in the sense of not requiring a public posting, but it must be loud in the sense of explicit expectation-setting. The single biggest predictor of a failed re-deployment, the Workplace Institute's data shows, is the employee saying in their exit interview that they did not know the role had changed until they were already doing it. Quiet hiring done well is a development conversation with a budget attached. Quiet hiring done badly is a surprise. And surprises, in workplaces, are the most expensive form of communication there is.

The macro picture is more sober. If half of all organisations are filling skill gaps internally rather than hiring, the labour market as we have known it is structurally reorganising. The next recession, when it comes, will not be a story of mass layoffs. It will be a story of quiet re-deployments, of roles disappearing without headlines, of people doing new work for the same pay and calling it growth because the alternative is to call it what it is. The job of the next decade is to make sure that what we call growth is actually growth — and that the quiet part of quiet hiring is its operational nature, not its human cost.

The second question is whether the trend is, in empirical terms, what its advocates claim. The LinkedIn data is impressive in scale but flattering in framing. The platform has every commercial incentive to position itself as the operating system of the future of work, and the headline numbers — half of all organisations are doing quiet hiring — are consistent with a definition of quiet hiring so broad that almost any internal mobility counts. The Workplace Institute's researchers have argued for a tighter definition: a re-deployment that is strategic, documented, and tied to a development plan is quiet hiring. A re-deployment that is opportunistic, undocumented, and unrewarded is something else, and they have taken to calling it quiet drift: the quiet expansion of someone's role without the quiet expansion of their compensation, status, or skills.

Quiet drift is, the research suggests, more prevalent than quiet hiring. In a recent survey of 4,200 knowledge workers across five countries, 38% reported doing work that was not in their job description at the time they were hired. Of those, only 22% had received a formal redefinition of their role. The remainder — 78% — were, in the Workplace Institute's taxonomy, drifting. The consequences are predictable. The drifters report lower engagement, higher burnout, and a significantly elevated intention to leave the organisation in the next twelve months. The employer, meanwhile, enjoys the labour without the cost of having hired for it. It is, in economic terms, a transfer of risk from the firm to the worker, and it is invisible in the headline employment statistics for the same reason that quiet hiring is — because nothing public has happened.

The second reason quiet hiring fails is that it assumes motion equals progress. A person who is moved from a stalling project to a different one is not necessarily growing; they may simply be carrying the same uncertainty to a new desk. The research team that studied this found that employees who were quietly hired reported higher levels of confusion about their career path than people who had stayed put and negotiated a clear next step. The lesson for managers is uncomfortable: the kind of growth that actually retains talent is visible, named, and mutually agreed — not a silent reshuffle that looks like opportunity from the outside.

readings.tag: Atlantic 风格 · 城市与心智
readings.title: The City That Taught Itself to Say I Don't Know
readings.subtitle: 一座城市如何学会了说「我不知道」
body: Helsinki does not, on the surface, seem like a city that has anything to teach the world. It is small — under seven hundred thousand people in the metro area. It is cold for half the year. Its architecture is the kind of understated modernism that visitors mistake for dullness. And yet, in 2024, when the Finnish capital asked its residents to help it design its next twenty-year plan, the process it used has begun to ripple outward, to city halls from Auckland to Albuquerque, as a quiet answer to a question many municipalities have stopped asking: what do we actually know, and what are we just guessing?

The Helsinki exercise, run through a platform called Decidim and adapted into Finnish as Avoin Helsinki, was not a consultation in the orthodox sense. The city did not publish a draft plan, ask residents to comment on it for six weeks, and then adjust the margins. Instead, it published a list of things it did not know. It published its open questions. It said, in effect: we are about to make decisions about transportation, housing, climate adaptation, and education. Here is what we have evidence on. Here is what we have anecdote on. Here is what we have nothing on. Help us tell the difference.

The response was not what most city planners expected. The submissions were not, by and large, demands. They were corrections. Residents read the city's open questions and pointed out places where the city's evidence was outdated, where the anecdote had moved on, where the silence in the city's knowledge was not because the issue was unimportant but because the city had never asked the right question. A twenty-year housing plan, it turned out, was being drafted on demographic projections from 2017. A cycling infrastructure plan was being drawn on a map of commute patterns that had not been updated since the pandemic. A library service plan assumed a population that no longer existed.

The deeper lesson, several of the researchers involved have argued, is about epistemic humility — the capacity of an institution to acknowledge the limits of what it knows. Most city planning processes operate on what the political theorist John Rawls once called the veil of competence: the implicit assumption that those in charge have done the work, and that public input is a matter of preference rather than evidence. Helsinki's exercise lifted that veil. It said: here is the evidence, here are its gaps, here is where your knowledge of your own neighbourhood is more reliable than ours. Tell us, in those places, what you see that we do not.

The shift in framing changed the psychology of participation. When a city asks residents to comment on a draft, the residents who show up are, by definition, the people who have time to read drafts. They are, statistically, older, better educated, more civically engaged, and more likely to be retired than the population as a whole. When a city asks residents to correct its open questions, the population that shows up is different. It includes people who know things the city does not — because they work the night shift, because they commute by a route the city's model does not capture, because they have a disabled child whose needs do not appear in any standard plan, because they are immigrants whose first language the city's outreach has never reached.

The Helsinki model has limits, of course. It requires a city that is willing to publish its gaps, which is to say a city that is confident enough in its own legitimacy to admit uncertainty. It requires staff who can distinguish a substantive correction from a partisan one. It requires a follow-through mechanism so that residents who take the time to submit corrections see those corrections actually show up in the next draft. None of these are trivial requirements. Many cities that have tried to copy the model have discovered that epistemic humility, like most kinds of humility, is easier to preach than to practise.

What the model does prove, however, is that the binary between top-down planning and bottom-up participation is a false one. The interesting question was never who gets to decide. It was who gets to define the boundary between what is known and what is not. When a city claims to know everything, it does not need its residents. When a city admits that it does not know everything, it discovers that its residents are not a problem to be managed but a resource to be deployed. Helsinki did not invent this insight. It just, for a moment, was honest enough to act on it.

There is a comparable phenomenon in corporate strategy, and it is worth naming because it explains why the Helsinki model is so hard to copy. Most firms run their annual planning on what could be called a veil of internal coherence: the implicit assumption that the strategy team has thought it through, that the leadership team has aligned on it, and that the organisation will execute against it. Like the city that publishes only finished plans, the firm that publishes only finished strategies denies its employees the opportunity to correct the premises on which the strategy rests. The employees execute against a plan that may have gone stale in the drafting, and the strategy team wonders, in the retrospective, why execution was so poor. The answer is the same as the city's: the people who know the plan is wrong were not asked.

The honest question for any organisation — public or private — is therefore not whether its plans are correct. They are almost certainly not, in detail, by the time they reach the people who have to execute them. The honest question is whether the organisation has the habit of admitting this, in public, in advance, so that the corrections can arrive before the execution rather than after it. Helsinki's exercise was, in this reading, not a consultation technique. It was a corporate governance innovation, applied to a city. The firm that borrows the technique — that publishes its open questions as well as its finished plans, that invites corrections in advance of execution — will not necessarily produce better plans on the first try. It will, however, produce plans that survive contact with the people who have to live with them. And that, in the end, is the only test of a plan that matters.

readings.tag: Vox 风格 · 心理与拖延
readings.title: Why You Procrastinate, and What to Do About It
readings.subtitle: 为什么你会拖延，以及真正的破解法
body: The standard story about procrastination is wrong. It says that procrastinators are lazy, that they lack self-discipline, that they need better time management, a stricter morning routine, a louder alarm clock. This story is appealing because it makes procrastination a character flaw — something you can fix by trying harder. It is also, according to the empirical research on the topic, almost entirely backwards.

The researchers who study procrastination — among them Tim Pychyl, Joseph Ferrari, and Fuschia Sirois — have spent two decades trying to understand what is actually happening when a person deliberately chooses to scroll through their phone instead of writing the report that is due in three hours. The answer they have converged on is this: procrastination is not a time management problem. It is an emotion regulation problem. People procrastinate because they are trying to manage a difficult feeling — usually anxiety, sometimes perfectionism, often a quiet dread that the work will not be good enough — and the temporary relief of avoidance feels, in the moment, better than the certain discomfort of confronting the task.

This is why the productivity advice that treats procrastination as a discipline problem fails. Telling an anxious person to use a Pomodoro timer is like telling a depressed person to cheer up. The advice is not wrong, exactly, but it is aimed at the wrong layer of the problem. The timer does not address the reason the person opened Instagram instead of the document. It just adds a guilt layer on top.

The first practical implication of the emotion regulation framing is that the question to ask when you find yourself procrastinating is not what should I be doing, but what am I avoiding feeling. The avoidance is the data. If you are scrolling instead of writing, the writing is triggering something — fear of judgement, fear of failure, fear of finding out you are not as good at the work as you want to be. The scroll is not the problem. The scroll is the symptom.

The second implication is that the most effective interventions for procrastination are not external — they are internal. They involve changing your relationship to the difficult feeling, not changing the environment in which you feel it. Pychyl's most quoted line in his lectures is that procrastination is the primordial sin of emotion regulation: the original way human beings learned to avoid pain. The treatment is therefore not to suppress the feeling — which makes it stronger — but to acknowledge it, name it, and then choose an action anyway, on the understanding that the action will be uncomfortable and the discomfort will pass.

This is, admittedly, easier to describe than to execute. A 2022 meta-analysis of procrastination interventions in the journal Psychological Bulletin found that the most effective single technique was something called implementation intentions — specific if-then plans that link a cue to an action in advance, so that the action does not require deliberation in the moment. The classic format is: if it is 9 a.m. on a Tuesday, I will open the document and write for twenty-five minutes. The point is not the twenty-five minutes. The point is that the decision has already been made, and the difficult feeling has lost the opportunity to intervene.

The third implication is about self-compassion. Sirois's research has repeatedly found that people who respond to their own procrastination with shame — who tell themselves they are lazy, who vow to do better next time, who punish themselves with guilt — procrastinate more in the future, not less. The shame triggers the same avoidance response the next time, and a vicious cycle is set. Self-compassion, by contrast, breaks the cycle. Treating the procrastination as a normal and understandable response to a difficult feeling — rather than a moral failure — makes it easier to return to the work without the additional burden of self-hatred.

The summary, then, is this. Procrastination is not a failure of willpower. It is a failure of strategy — the strategy of trying to manage difficult feelings by avoiding the work that triggers them. The fix is not more discipline. The fix is to recognise what you are avoiding, to plan around the avoidance in advance, and to treat the moments you slip with the same patience you would offer a friend. The work will still be hard. The deadline will still loom. But the internal narrative changes from I am a lazy person who cannot finish things to I am a person who finds this work hard, and I am choosing to do it anyway. The first narrative makes you hide. The second one lets you start.

The cultural obstacle to this framing is the Protestant work ethic in its current, productivity-bro form. The assumption is that discipline is the thing you build by suffering through uncomfortable work, and that the feeling of not wanting to do the work is a signal of weakness to be overcome. The research on procrastination suggests the opposite. The feeling of not wanting to do the work is a signal of information — information about what the work means to you, what you fear about it, what part of it is triggering a threat response. Discipline, in the traditional sense, is what you use to suppress the signal. The alternative is to use the signal. The feeling of resistance at the start of a task is data, not a defect.

This is, admittedly, a less satisfying story than the discipline one. The discipline story promises that if you try hard enough, you will stop feeling the resistance. The research says you will not. You will stop noticing it, which is a different thing, and the cost of not noticing it is paid in burnout, in chronic under-performance, in the slow erosion of engagement that defines so many mid-career professionals in knowledge work. The work of noticing is uncomfortable. The work of not noticing is worse. The choice, in the end, is not between discipline and permissiveness. It is between two kinds of discomfort — the discomfort of seeing what you are avoiding, and the discomfort of carrying what you have refused to see.

readings.tag: New Yorker 风格 · 第三空间
readings.title: The Quiet Return of the Third Place
readings.subtitle: 「第三空间」正在悄悄回归
body: The term third place was coined by the sociologist Ray Oldenburg, in his 1989 book The Great Good Place, to describe the hangouts that exist outside the two dominant environments of adult life — the home and the workplace. The café, the barber shop, the public library, the diner, the local park, the corner pub. These are the places where, in Oldenburg's argument, a civic life is forged. They are where you encounter people you did not intend to meet, where conversation happens without an agenda, where the bonds of trust that make a neighbourhood work are quietly maintained.

For the first two decades of this century, the thesis of the third place was that it was dying. The causes were familiar: the collapse of local retail, the rise of remote work, the migration of social life to platforms, the gentrification of public space, the escalating cost of leisure in cities. The coffee chain replaced the café. The algorithm replaced the serendipity. The headphones replaced the stranger on the next stool. The third place, in this telling, was being substituted by something cheaper and quieter and, the critics argued, much worse.

What the critics did not predict is that the third place would rebound, and that when it did, it would look decidedly different from its pre-digital incarnation. The data from 2023 onwards is striking. Independent coffee shops in the United States grew by 12% between 2022 and 2025. Board game cafés, a category that did not really exist before 2010, now number more than four thousand in North America. Listening bars — small venues built around a high-end sound system and a strict no-talking-during-the-music rule — have become one of the fastest-growing formats in hospitality. Running clubs, book clubs, pottery studios, neighbourhood kitchens: the third place is not vanishing. It is mutating.

The new third place is, in several respects, a deliberate construction. Where the old one was incidental — a corner pub that happened to be at the corner — the new one is curated. It is a place someone decided to build, with a specific aesthetic, a specific set of rules, and a specific promise about what the experience will and will not include. The listening bar promises silence. The board game café promises analogue play. The running club promises company at a pace the slowest member can maintain. The third place is being re-engineered for an audience that has spent a decade on platforms and is now, with a vengeance, looking for the things the platforms do not provide.

The list of things the platforms do not provide is, when you write it down, striking. They do not provide ambient presence — the experience of being near other people without needing to perform for them. They do not provide unscripted encounter — the meeting of a person you did not expect to meet, in a context you did not arrange. They do not provide silence — actual, shared, two-people-in-a-room silence, which is one of the most underrated forms of human intimacy. They do not provide the small frictions of public life — the queue at the bar, the apology when you bump someone's chair, the eye contact with the stranger across the table. These are the things the third place, in its old and new forms, is being re-engineered to restore.

This is not to romanticise the new third place. It has its exclusivity problems — a tasting-menu listening bar is not a democratic institution. It has its aesthetic pressures — the third place now has a brand identity, an Instagram aesthetic, and a price point, and the trade-offs that come with all three. It has, like the old third place, the problem of who feels welcome and who does not. The corner pub of Oldenburg's 1989 was not, in retrospect, as universally warm as the memories suggest. The new third place is no more innocent.

But the underlying hunger is real, and it is not going away. Generations who came of age entirely on platforms are discovering that the platforms were not, in the end, a substitute for the third place. They were a distraction from the absence of it. The café is back. The bar is back. The library is, in many cities, unexpectedly thriving. The third place did not die. It went away for a while, and now, in forms its original theorist would not quite recognise, it is coming back. The sociologist in me wants to resist the narrative of return. The resident in me is just grateful to have somewhere to go on a Tuesday night that is not my apartment and not my laptop.

The third observation is about timing. The new third place is, in almost every case, a post-pandemic phenomenon. It did not exist, in its current form, before 2020. It emerged from a specific historical condition: a decade of platform mediated social life, a pandemic that removed the in-person default, and a subsequent period of rebuilding in which the people doing the rebuilding were explicit about what they missed and what they did not. The third place of 2026 is the answer to a specific question: what would I pay to recover, from the pre-platform era, that the platforms did not replace? The answer, in city after city, is the same thing: presence without performance, encounter without agenda, silence without isolation.

It is tempting to end on the note that the third place is back, and that this is, on the whole, a good thing. I am hesitant to do so, because the back is not the same as what was there before. The new third place is curated, priced, branded, and institutionally fragile in ways the old one was not. The old corner pub survived recessions because it was cheap to run, because its patrons drank what it served, and because its social function was obvious to everyone who walked in. The new third place is vulnerable to rent increases, to algorithm shifts on the platforms that drive discovery, to changes in consumer taste that are faster than the rent cycle. It may not last. But what it reveals, while it lasts, is that the human need it serves is real, and that the platforms, for all their convenience, did not make the need go away. They made it quiet. The third place, in its new forms, is what the need sounds like when it is loud again.

dialogs.title: At the check-in counter
dialogs.goal: 练习护照/行李/座位相关表达，从容应对值机

lines.en: Good morning. May I see your passport and booking reference, please?
lines.zh: 早上好，请出示您的护照和预订编号。

lines.en: Sure, here you are. I'd like a window seat if possible.
lines.zh: 好的，给您。如果可以的话我想要靠窗的座位。

lines.en: I can arrange that. Are you checking in any bags today?
lines.zh: 可以安排。您今天有要托运的行李吗？

lines.en: Just one suitcase. Does it meet the weight limit?
lines.zh: 就一个行李箱。它超重了吗？

lines.en: It's within the limit. Your boarding pass is ready — gate 22, boarding at 10:40.
lines.zh: 在限额内。您的登机牌好了——22 号登机口，10:40 登机。

dialogs.title: Small talk at a conference
dialogs.goal: 用自然的破冰句开启商务对话，并过渡到合作话题

lines.en: Hi, I don't think we've met. I'm Echo, from the consumer insights team.
lines.zh: 你好，我们好像还没见过。我是 Echo，来自消费者洞察团队。

lines.en: Nice to meet you. I work on product strategy. What brings you to this session?
lines.zh: 很高兴认识你。我做产品策略。你为什么来听这场？

lines.en: I'm exploring how AI is changing our research methods. Have you seen anything useful today?
lines.zh: 我在研究 AI 如何改变我们的研究方法。你今天有看到什么有用的吗？

lines.en: Actually, yes — a talk on real-time consumer signals. We should compare notes sometime.
lines.zh: 其实有——一个关于实时消费者信号的演讲。我们应该找个时间交流一下。

lines.en: I'd love that. Let's grab coffee after the keynote.
lines.zh: 太好了。主题演讲后我们喝杯咖啡吧。

dialogs.title: Checking into a hotel
dialogs.goal: 掌握入住登记、特殊需求与Wi-Fi等常用句

lines.en: Good evening. Do you have a reservation under the name Lee?
lines.zh: 晚上好。请问有预订在 Lee 名下吗？

lines.en: Yes, for two nights. Is breakfast included?
lines.zh: 有的，住两晚。含早餐吗？

lines.en: It is — served from 7 to 10. Could I have a room on a higher floor, away from the elevator?
lines.zh: 含的——7 点到 10 点供应。可以安排高一点、远离电梯的房间吗？

lines.en: Certainly. Here's your key card, and the Wi-Fi password is on this slip.
lines.zh: 当然可以。这是您的房卡，Wi-Fi 密码在这张纸上。

dialogs.title: Ordering with dietary needs
dialogs.goal: 清晰表达过敏/忌口，避免误会

lines.en: Welcome! Have you decided what you'd like to order?
lines.zh: 欢迎！您决定好点什么了吗？

lines.en: Not yet. I'm allergic to peanuts — could you tell me which dishes are safe?
lines.zh: 还没。我对花生过敏——能告诉我哪些菜是安全的吗？

lines.en: Of course. The grilled fish and the vegetable soup are both nut-free. I'll note the allergy for the kitchen.
lines.zh: 当然。烤鱼和蔬菜汤都不含坚果。我会在厨房单上标注过敏。

lines.en: Perfect, thank you. Could I also get that without spicy sauce?
lines.zh: 太好了，谢谢。那份可以不放辣酱吗？

dialogs.title: Talking about AI at work
dialogs.goal: 用职场商务英语表达对 AI 的看法与担忧

lines.en: Have you tried the new AI assistant? It's been a game-changer for my drafts.
lines.zh: 你试过新的 AI 助手了吗？它彻底改变了我写草稿的方式。

lines.en: I have, but I'm cautious. I double-check everything it produces.
lines.zh: 试过，但我比较谨慎。它生成的东西我都会复核。

lines.en: Fair enough. I see it as a starting point, not the final answer.
lines.zh: 有道理。我把它当作起点，而不是最终答案。

lines.en: Exactly. The human touch still matters most with our clients.
lines.zh: 没错。对咱们的客户来说，人情味依然最重要。
